{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"cb5aecc0bb28733dca23c2db17bdfd67ca7543b31159b6d8dccb0ef3f2565a86","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:64","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Traffic signals, signs and markings confusables and continuation details","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: flashing yellow versus flashing red, passive versus active railroad warnings, speed bumps versus speed humps, and continuation details on pedestrian buttons, lane markings, HOV lanes, slow-moving vehicles, rumble strips and roundabouts","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: flashing yellow versus flashing red, passive versus active railroad warnings, speed bumps versus speed humps, and continuation details on pedestrian buttons, lane markings, HOV lanes, slow-moving vehicles, rumble strips and roundabouts
Confusable pairs among signals, signs and markings, followed by continuation facts the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec15-R01 | anchor: A02
A flashing yellow light only asks you to slow down and take care, but a flashing red light requires a full stop before going on when safe. [A02]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable flashing yellow versus flashing red.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-R02 | anchor: A07
Pavement markings, signs and crossbucks are passive railroad warning devices, while flashing red lights, ringing bells and lowered gates are active warnings. [A07]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; confusable passive versus active warnings.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R03 | anchor: A08
A speed bump is a low ridge across the street, while a speed hump is a longer, flatter version. [A08]
Why it matters: group speed control; confusable bump versus hump.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0220]

FACT_ID: sec15-R04 | anchor: A07
With a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line side by side, pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and finish the pass before the dashes turn solid. [A07]
Why it matters: group road markings; confusable solid versus dashed yellow.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R05 | anchor: A06
Double solid yellow and white lines prohibit passing, so never cross a solid yellow line to pass, stay in your lane and keep right when driving slowly. [A06]
Why it matters: group road markings; confusable double solid versus single solid.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-R06 | anchor: A03
At signals with pedestrian push buttons, pressing the button soon changes the flow so the side street gets a longer green. [A03]
Why it matters: group pedestrian signals; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0215]

FACT_ID: sec15-R07 | anchor: A03
Pedestrian crossing and bicycle warning signs may be standard yellow or an optional yellow-green, and they tell drivers to share the road with and yield to pedestrians and cyclists. [A03]
Why it matters: group warning signs; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0215]

FACT_ID: sec15-R08 | anchor: A04
A yellow diamond is also used for roadway hazard and railroad crossing warning signs. [A04]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; confusable yellow diamond versus round yellow railroad sign.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-R09 | anchor: A05
Near road work, control your following distance and reaction time, read and follow the signs, be ready to slow or stop, and watch for workers and moving machinery. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0217]

FACT_ID: sec15-R10 | anchor: A05
Reduced speed limit signs are posted alongside orange work zone signs. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0217]

FACT_ID: sec15-R11 | anchor: A06
Road arrows used with other signs show the direction a driver must take from that lane, and white dashed lines separate lanes on multi-lane highways. [A06]
Why it matters: group road markings; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-R12 | anchor: A07
Edge lines separate the shoulder from the travel lane and mark the edge of the highway, and yellow edge lines do the same job. [A07]
Why it matters: group road markings; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R13 | anchor: A07
Where no stop line is painted, stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires you to stop, and where a white stop line exists, stop at it. [A07]
Why it matters: group road markings; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R14 | anchor: A07
White special pavement markings such as STOP AHEAD, SCHOOL and RXR alert drivers to special conditions ahead. [A07]
Why it matters: group road markings; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R15 | anchor: A07
White diamonds on signs or painted in the lane mark high occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes reserved for certain vehicles or for vehicles carrying several riders, and posted signs give the operating hours. [A07]
Why it matters: group road markings; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R16 | anchor: A07
A fluorescent, reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle marks a slow-moving vehicle, such as farm or construction equipment on a public highway. [A07]
Why it matters: group special signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0219]

FACT_ID: sec15-R17 | anchor: A08
Rumble strips vibrate the wheel and make noise to warn of a decision point ahead or wake a dozing driver; they do not damage the vehicle and usually come with a caution sign. [A08]
Why it matters: group speed control; misconception rumble strips harm the car.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0220]

FACT_ID: sec15-R18 | anchor: A08
A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection around a center island, and because traffic enters and exits only by right turns, severe crashes are greatly reduced. [A08]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0220]
